Last week, news broke that hackers had stolen $6.3 billion from wallets on Binance, the most popular cryptocurrency exchange in the world. The company was able to freeze about nearly $3 billion of it, but the attack quickly made headlines, and rightfully so, as the largest financial heist in human history.
At the time, I suspected, along with security researcher Christopher Lopez and plenty of others, that this could have very well started on a Mac. As Lopez pointed out, the $1.5 billion Bybit heist last year also began on a developer’s Mac. On top of that, Macs are hugely popular among DevOps engineers and crypto folks, and they’ve been on the receiving end of a steady stream of malware and social engineering campaigns over the past few years.
I can now say any suspicions that this heist originated on Mac were right. I’m still in a state of shock. Dazed not by the amount stolen, but how the said hackers did so using the same ol’ social engineering tricks they’ve been using for years. No sophisticated multi-milllion dollar underground zero-day here.
Yesterday, Binance published a more detailed breakdown of the attack. The company never actually says “Mac,” but the malware it published targeted /opt/homebrew, which is where Homebrew lives on Apple silicon Macs. In other words, this was almost certainly an M-series MacBook.
The attack basically transpired in two steps.
According to Binance, in June this year, a DevOps engineer working on Wallet searched for an AI coding tool and downloaded a malicious clone of the Homebrew installer in Google Search. Binance claims it caught it early and stopped any damage. However, what it didn’t know was that it allowed the attackers to learn which employees worked on its wallets. This was phase 1.
Fast forward a few months to September, a different engineer who, you guessed it, worked on wallets for Binance, was lured into a fake job interview. As these sort of social engineering attacks normally go, they told to run a coding “assignment” on their work computer. This was not caught by Binance security, and on October 29, the world learned that hackers (now widely speculated as North Korean hackers) walked off with billions.
Of course, most of what we know so far comes directly from Binance, so if you’re looking for more details on exactly how this happened, you’ll likely be left empty-handed.
It’s important to note here though, none of these two attack vectors are new. Back in early 2025, I wrote about fake Homebrew ads at the top of Google Search pushing Atomic Stealer to Mac users. Binance only says the engineer found his installer through “a search engine.” Of course, I can’t confirm it was a sponsored ad, but if history tells us anything…
This is a rather uncomfortable situation for Apple to be in. The largest financial heist in history happen on Mac last week, though to be fair, there’s no security feature that can stop a developer from running a script he wants to run.
Sure, the Terminal paste warnings introduced in macOS 26.4 could have helped here. But realistically, if someone’s convinced they’re doing a coding test for a job they really want, a warning pop-up probably isn’t going to stop them.
Here’s what that warning looks like:
I’m having Christopher Lopez (@L0Psec) a professional macOS reverse engineer back on the Security Bite Podcast this week to talk about the Binance situation with me. Follow the show so you don’t miss that.
Security Bite is 9to5Mac’s weekly deep dive into the world of Apple security. Each week, Arin Waichulis unpacks new threats, privacy concerns, vulnerabilities, and more, shaping an ecosystem of over 2 billion devices. results.summary:
Hackers stole $6.3 billion from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance after compromising a developer’s Mac through social engineering tactics and a malicious coding assignment disguised as a job interview.

### Key Points
- Attackers successfully exfiltrated $6.3 billion from Binance, marking the largest financial heist in history.
- The breach originated on an Apple silicon Mac, evidenced by malware targeting the /opt/homebrew directory.
- Hackers utilized a two-phase social engineering campaign, starting with a malicious Homebrew installer in June and a fake job interview in September.
- Security experts suspect North Korean hackers orchestrated the attack by tricking a DevOps engineer into running a malicious coding script.
- Binance managed to freeze approximately $3 billion of the stolen funds following the October 29 discovery of the theft.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the growing vulnerability of enterprise environments where developers frequently use macOS for high-stakes financial infrastructure. It demonstrates that even sophisticated organizations remain susceptible to basic social engineering, emphasizing the need for stricter endpoint security beyond standard operating system warnings.

results.title: The fight for tech accountability starts now
results.author: Adi Robertson
results.content:
When Donald Trump began his second term as president, Silicon Valley gratefully embraced moral nihilism. Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and more collectively donated millions to Trump’s inauguration fund to ensure his favor in a new era of gangster tech regulation. Meta overhauled its content policy to allow calling gay people mentally ill and women property. Elon Musk started throwing Nazi salutes — yes, allegedly, but he would soon be posting nonstop about protecting the white race from extinction, so that’s the most fragile of fig leafs.
The fight for tech accountability starts now
Trump is still in office, but the era of gangster tech regulation needs to end.
As of mere months ago, this was working out pretty well for them. The Trump administration took a mostly hands-off regulatory approach, particularly in the burgeoning field of AI. It decided to simply not enforce a divest-or-ban law against TikTok (something that was originally Trump’s own idea!), leading TikTok to thank Trump by name in its app. A Republican-led Congress was too dysfunctional to pass the tech regulations it did want. The Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission still pursued some existing Big Tech lawsuits, but the flood of high-profile investigations we saw under the Biden administration — and the first Trump administration — slowed markedly. Musk functionally ran the US government for a few months.
And beyond simple regulatory favors, Trump, once a vituperative critic of Big Tech, became joined at the hip with it. Tech CEOs prominently attended his inauguration, and their companies showered him with ballroom donations and gold gewgaws. The White House hosted the reveal of the Stargate Project, OpenAI’s massive data center plan. The US Army created a special detachment for executives from Meta, Palantir, OpenAI, and Thinking Machines Lab, and Trump tapped tech leaders as advisers. He ordered an entire technology renamed because he thought it would make the AI industry look better, and the industry duly fell in line.
Now, these companies’ all-in support is looking awfully risky.
Yesterday’s midterm elections were a historic disaster for Republicans. Democrats not only won the House and Senate, they flipped seats that were considered long shots or downright impossible six months ago: Texas has a Democratic senator and a Democratic governor. Trump is still president, but in Congress, Democrats will be empowered to launch investigations and haul tech execs into hearings, and they’ll have leverage to negotiate over budget and defense bills. And the electoral backlash, of course, bodes ill for Republicans’ prospects of holding the presidency in 2028.
Americans are angry. Trump and his administration’s actions invited much of that anger: his pointless trade wars, a senseless actual war, adviser Stephen Miller’s brutal and lawless immigration crackdowns, and much more. But the tech industry is an easy target, too. Its hyperscale data centers became a flashpoint in numerous midterm races, and public trepidation about AI — a technology whose defenders argue it will destroy countless jobs and possibly kill everyone — is high.
There’s a lot of dirt for newly empowered Democratic lawmakers to investigate. Google may strenuously deny a specious $24.5 million legal settlement was a bribe, for instance, but even as the minority party, Democrats rightly raised questions about it. Trump has enriched himself through connections with the cryptocurrency industry and in the process backed off investigating crypto fraud. Musk may have benefited financially in countless ways from his ties to Trump, and that’s on top of his reckless, destructive, and allegedly illegal actions with DOGE, which devastated parts of the federal government and likely led to hundreds of thousands of deaths.
But tech is so overdue for a reckoning that the very term “reckoning” has started to feel like a joke. AI companies have been making vague “please regulate us” overtures for years, and it’s time to take their incessant doom-bragging seriously — by, for instance, using subpoena powers to push them on their responsibility for “rogue” AI agent hacks. Actual legislation likely won’t happen with Trump in office, but if there’s private information that suggests companies should bear legal liability, congressional investigations can help dig it up.
The fight over data centers so far has mostly taken place at a local level, and newly elected Democrats at the state level will likely keep the pushback high. Given how many Republicans hate hyperscale centers too, a Democratic majority could also make a serious bid for federal action — at the very least, they could put a bill on Trump’s desk and force him to own his unpopular pro-data-center stance by vetoing it. And far more easily, they can stymie Trump’s push to override local regulations. Trump’s long-favored state AI law moratorium, which Republicans have tried to sneak through Congress multiple times, seems gone for good.
The fight over data centers will probably only escalate from here
Democrats shouldn’t replicate Republicans’ bad-faith attacks on the tech industry during the Biden administration, which saw Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) weaponize congressional committee powers to accuse social media platforms of censorship. But they shouldn’t be afraid to crack open the alliance between a lawless, grift-friendly administration and a powerful industry that paid him handsomely and was rewarded with regulatory favor. They’re also poised to figure out just how much Trump and his administration — where figures like FCC chair Brendan Carr display contempt for basic constitutional rights, to a point even some Republicans can’t support — have threatened that industry with punishment if it didn’t support him.
Unfortunately, even with an undeniable mandate for change, there’s a huge risk that lawmakers will deliver exactly what they have for the past decade in tech reform: almost nothing. Despite the best efforts of some reformers in Congress, the US has perennially failed to pass even laws with bipartisan support, like antitrust overhauls and a data privacy framework. Hauling tech execs into court creates good sound bites, but without any real action, it only cements the idea that the government is useless.
Democrats probably will soon have tech execs courting them as well. Meta, the fairest-weather friend in Silicon Valley, appeared to be already hedging its bets before the election. They’ll be tempted to retreat into the friendly relationship they had with tech companies during the Obama and early Trump years. But it’s too late to go back. Even at its best, the tech industry needs a check on its power — and the past two years have shown it at its worst.
results.summary:
Major technology companies face increased political risk and potential congressional scrutiny following historic Democratic gains in the midterm elections, which threaten their close alliance with the Trump administration.

### Key Points
- Democrats secured control of both the House and Senate, empowering them to launch investigations into tech industry practices and regulatory favors.
- Silicon Valley firms, including Google, Meta, and OpenAI, previously donated millions to the Trump inauguration and received favorable regulatory treatment.
- Public and political backlash is mounting against hyperscale data centers and the rapid, unregulated expansion of artificial intelligence.
- Lawmakers are expected to scrutinize potential conflicts of interest involving cryptocurrency, federal contracts, and the administration's hands-off approach to tech oversight.
- Legislative efforts to override local data center regulations and impose AI moratoriums face significant new hurdles under the shifted congressional balance.

### Why it Matters
The shift in congressional power signals a potential end to the era of "gangster tech regulation" that characterized the recent alignment between Silicon Valley and the White House. This transition forces tech companies to navigate a more hostile regulatory environment while risking their previous influence over federal policy and industry standards.

results.title: Abnormal AI's new CMO says 'safe is boring' and is ditching the B2B marketing playbook
results.author: Lara O'Reilly
results.content:
Cybersecurity startup Abnormal AI wants its marketing to be anything but ordinary.
Abnormal AI exclusively told CMO Insider on Wednesday that it has appointed Don Jeter as its chief marketing officer.
In an interview, Jeter said he has big ambitions to use unconventional marketing techniques as part of a plan to build Abnormal AI into a "household name" brand.
"I want my nephew, who is 14, and my parents to know Abnormal," Jeter said. "I want to be the most talked-about cybersecurity company in 2027."
Jeter said that's why he intends to throw out the traditional business-to-business marketing playbook, which often focuses on features and functions, and instead plans to create "cultural moments" that will capture the attention of all kinds of consumers beyond its CISO target audience.
Founded in 2018, Abnormal made its name using behavioral AI to detect email security threats. It has since expanded the technology to help companies spot unusual activity in employees' digital accounts and logins, and is increasingly applying the same approach to securing organizations' use of AI tools. The company was valued at $5.1 billion after a $250 million Series D funding round in 2024.
One of Jeter's near-term challenges is resetting the narrative that Abnormal is only an email security company.
He'll be attempting to do so in a noisy market, competing for mindshare against the marketing heft of trillion-dollar tech giants and buzzy frontier AI companies, as well as the cybersecurity vendors jostling for chief information security officers' budgets.
"Right now, in this market, you've got to build trust and awareness before the sales conversation starts," Jeter said. "If you do brand marketing correctly, everything else gets easier; it signals to the market you are winning."
While he wanted to keep his specific plans under wraps for now, Jeter said out-of-home advertising and other IRL activations are likely to play key roles in Abnormal AI's marketing mix.
"We want to create stuff that people naturally want to share and participate in," Jeter said. "With great marketing, you never have to ask your employees to 'please share and retweet.'"
B2B brands are increasingly taking a more business-to-consumer marketing approach. Salesforce and Adobe hold their glitzy Dreamforce and MAX conferences. Autodesk has a string of major sports team partnerships and splurged to advertise on the Las Vegas Sphere. Elsewhere, Ramp enlisted former pro skater Tony Hawk for a comedic campaign that culminated with him dropping in and skating on a ramp during a live event outside the New York Stock Exchange and around the trading floor.
"A B2B buyer is still a person who remembers a great story, and in a category where nearly every company is promising smarter AI, tighter security, or faster results, IRL connection gives people a reason to remember one brand over another," said Steve Nottingham, CEO of the commerce experience agency RSM&, about Jeter's plans for Abnormal AI.
Nottingham said CMOs who want to execute these kinds of activations need to start with a clear objective, an idea that could only come from their brand, a defined audience, a parallel content strategy that allows for amplification, and measurement that clearly connects the buzz to brand awareness and the sales pipeline.
"Done thoughtfully, a real-world moment can work harder than almost any other line in the budget, because the conversation it starts keeps going well beyond the day itself," Nottingham said.
Jeter has experience in this area. As CMO of cybersecurity startup Torq, he built the brand through deliberately offbeat marketing campaigns. Torq sponsored Monster Jam's nationwide tour for its "Torq, not torque" campaign, then brought a 20-foot inflatable skeleton and an on-site tattoo bus to the 2026 RSAC cybersecurity conference.
"B2B marketing, in general, has played it safe for a very long time, and what we are seeing is that's no longer working in today's culture and scarce attention economy," Jeter said. "Safe is boring, and boring is invisible."
results.summary:
Cybersecurity startup Abnormal AI has appointed former Torq executive Don Jeter as its new chief marketing officer to lead a strategy focused on unconventional, consumer-facing brand building.

### Key Points
- Abnormal AI appointed Don Jeter as CMO to transition the company from a niche email security provider to a recognizable household brand by 2027.
- The company, founded in 2018, reached a $5.1 billion valuation following a $250 million Series D funding round in 2024.
- Jeter plans to move away from traditional B2B marketing by utilizing out-of-home advertising and "cultural moments" to capture attention beyond the CISO audience.
- The strategy aims to differentiate Abnormal AI in a crowded market dominated by trillion-dollar tech giants and numerous cybersecurity competitors.
- Jeter previously gained industry attention at Torq by executing offbeat campaigns, including sponsoring Monster Jam and hosting a tattoo bus at a major conference.

### Why it Matters
This shift reflects a growing trend where B2B companies adopt consumer-style marketing to build brand awareness and trust before initiating sales conversations. By prioritizing memorable, real-world experiences, Abnormal AI hopes to cut through the noise of a saturated cybersecurity market and establish a distinct identity.

results.title: The Lawyer Holding Big Tech Accountable by ‘Beating the Tar Out of Them’ in Court
results.author: Kate Taylor
results.content:
As social media giants face allegations that they fail to protect users, attorney Mark Lanier is grappling with the question: What would it actually take to hold companies accountable?
"I think it just takes beating the tar out of them," Lanier told WIRED senior correspondent Lauren Goode at the WIRED World Fair on Wednesday.
Lanier was the lead attorney in the first social media addiction case to go to trial, which resulted in a verdict against Meta and Google in March. The plaintiff was awarded $6 million in damages—a symbolic victory but a rounding error in terms of the tech giants’ bottom lines.
Lanier said lawsuits in which attorneys general represent their states have the potential to orchestrate significant change, alongside greater financial repercussions. In a case that went to trial in August, attorneys general across several states—including Arkansas, where Lanier’s firm served as outside counsel—accused Meta of failing to protect young social media users.
A few days into the trial, Meta agreed to a settlement of up to $16.7 billion, to be paid out to 51 US states and territories. The social media giant also pledged to make changes on how teenagers use Instagram and Facebook, such as a default two-hour time limit. (TikTok agreed to similar limits as part of a settlement in Alabama in September.)
A $1.7 trillion-dollar company like Meta can treat such settlements and verdicts as the cost of doing business, even if the costs climb into the billions. But these cases also have more nebulous repercussions. They impact how the public—and companies’ own employees—feel about the platforms. Lanier said that, in addition to wins in court, change can come from people understanding companies’ actions and demanding accountability.
“I am not here because I'm bored on a Wednesday,” Lanier said from the WIRED World Fair stage. “I'm here because I want everybody to know what these companies do—because that type of pressure will help change everything.”
results.summary:
Attorney Mark Lanier argues that aggressive litigation and public pressure are essential to holding major social media companies accountable for failing to protect young users from platform harms.

### Key Points
- Attorney Mark Lanier secured a $6 million verdict against Meta and Google in the first social media addiction trial.
- Meta agreed to a $16.7 billion settlement with 51 U.S. states and territories in August to resolve claims regarding youth safety.
- New platform safety measures include default two-hour daily time limits for teenagers on Instagram, Facebook, and TikTok.
- Lanier emphasizes that public awareness and employee sentiment are critical factors in forcing long-term corporate policy changes.

### Why it Matters
These legal actions signal a shift in how regulators and courts address the societal impact of social media algorithms on minors. While multibillion-dollar settlements represent significant financial penalties, the broader industry impact depends on whether these mandates successfully alter platform design and user safety standards.

results.title: Dow jumps over 1,000 points in response to Democrats' control of Congress
results.author: Grace O'Donnell
results.content:
Stock market today: Dow surges 1,500 points in best day of 2026, S&P 500 and Nasdaq rally after historic midterm election
US stocks jumped on Wednesday after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in a seismic midterm election, paving the way for a divided government.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) rose 3%, or over 1,500 points, marking its best single-day performance since President Trump paused a sweeping tariff rollout in April 2025. The S&P 500 (^GSPC) climbed 1.6%. The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) traded up by 1.4% amid a post-election relief rally.
Markets swiftly repriced a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate — and the potential for ballot measures and newly elected officials to restrict data center construction. Chip stocks, including Nvidia (NVDA) and Micron (MU), fell. Meanwhile, other parts of the tech sector offset some of those losses, with Apple (AAPL) and Microsoft (MSFT) each hitting all-time highs.
Oil prices plunged as the midterm election outcome also raised hopes for an end to the war in the Middle East. Brent crude oil futures (BZ=F) dropped 8% to around $95 per barrel.
Investors will also be watching in the coming weeks for policy actions on housing and pharmaceuticals in the aftermath of the election. As Yahoo Finance's Jared Blikre pointed out on Tuesday, midterm elections have a history of shaping stock performance in the near term but don't tend to move markets much over the long term.
On the economic front, ISM and S&P data showed that US services activity expanded at a slower pace in October as businesses continued to grapple with elevated costs. Private-sector hiring, meanwhile, continued to show strength in October as an ADP report indicated "pretty solid job growth."
Earnings continue to roll in. AMD (AMD) posted a Q3 earnings beat, while McDonald's (MCD) grappled with slowing same-store sales growth. Duolingo (DUOL) stock soared over 30% on strong user growth.
- Bitcoin rises above $80,000 as investors go risk-on Bitcoin (BTC-USD) jumped 3%, and ethereum (ETH-USD) also rallied on Wednesday after Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress, even as the midterm outcome could complicate the crypto industry's efforts to pass favorable legislation. Bitcoin touched a six-week low before recovering to just above $80,000, moving back above its 50-day moving average. Ethereum also rallied, gaining 7% to trade above $2,400 as US equities broadly rallied and investors went risk-on.
results.summary:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average surged over 1,500 points as U.S. markets rallied following a Democratic sweep of Congress in the 2026 midterm elections.

### Key Points
- The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 3%, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.6% and 1.4% respectively.
- Brent crude oil futures dropped 8% to $95 per barrel amid investor optimism regarding potential resolutions to conflicts in the Middle East.
- Tech sector performance was mixed, with Apple and Microsoft hitting record highs while chipmakers like Nvidia and Micron declined.
- Bitcoin recovered to trade above $80,000, and Ethereum gained 7% to surpass $2,400 following the election results.
- Duolingo shares jumped over 30% on strong user growth, while McDonald's reported slowing same-store sales.

### Why it Matters
The market's positive reaction to a divided government highlights investor relief regarding the conclusion of midterm uncertainty. While historical data suggests these election-driven rallies are often short-lived, the shift in legislative control will likely influence future policy decisions on housing, pharmaceuticals, and data center regulation.

results.title: Apple Wins Big in CNET’s People’s Picks Awards for Its MacBooks
results.author: Dashia Milden
results.content:
Of all of the laptop brands to choose from, CNET readers say Apple’s signature MacBooks really live up to the hype.
We recently surveyed CNET readers as part of our People’s Picks awards to find out what they think about their laptop and the brand behind it to help you make a more sound choice on the laptop you may be considering over the holidays. We listed several well-known names, including Dell, Lenovo — and Apple. We asked about everything that matters most on a daily basis, like battery life, durability and even its performance for handling tasks like gaming and graphics. Out of 10 categories, Apple swept up eight of the awards and claimed the overall winner for CNET’s People’s Picks award.
Here’s what readers say Apple gets right when it comes to its laptops, what the experts think about Apple’s landslide win and other brands worth considering.
More from CNET
CNET’s Overall People’s Pick for Laptops Winner: Apple
Apple wins the overall award in CNET’s People’s Picks, and also takes home the overall satisfaction rating, with 74.2% of Apple users saying they’re extremely satisfied with their laptop. In comparison, 22.5% say they’re satisfied — bringing Apple to a near-perfect overall satisfaction score of 96.7%.
Apple’s overall impression also speaks to other awards it wins from CNET readers, including high ratings for its impressive battery life, display quality and high-quality build. All of those categories and more sum up Apple’s brand loyalty nod, with 68% of MacBook owners saying they would buy the same laptop and model from Apple again.
Premium laptop
How much are people paying for MacBooks? CNET found that 43.5% of Apple users paid at least $1,500. Until earlier in 2026, the MacBook Air was Apple’s entry-level laptop, priced at least $1,299. The introduction of the budget-friendly MacBook Neo brought that down to a more reasonable $699. However, despite Apple’s laptops being more expensive than those from other brands, they still ranked high for their value proposition. Part of the reason for that is that MacBooks received high marks for hardware reliability. “Apple’s MacBooks might cost more than the average laptop, but their premium build quality means they’re built for the long haul,” said Matt Elliott, CNET’s laptop editor.
If you plan to have your laptop for a while, you may be impressed by other features that make work easier and faster, like its M-series central processing unit for task management and AI capabilities, great battery life and a one-of-a-kind operating system — currently MacOS 27. All of the features and specifications bundled together make Apple’s perception as a high-end laptop worth the investment for long-term satisfaction.
Cost for value
Apple clinches a near-perfect score for its value perception. According to our survey results, 44% of Apple users said their MacBook has exceptional value. Others say their MacBook is worth what they paid for it (50.9%) — for a total positive score of 94.6%.
Digging deeper into Apple’s cost-to-value rating, 81.8% of Apple owners paid at least $1,000 for their laptops, which may seem costly, but Apple users seem OK with the price. That could be because, even though Apple has only three laptop models in a handful of sizes in its lineup, each one delivers solid performance and storage.
Take Apple’s proprietary processing chips, for example — each upgrade since the M1 release has improved the laptop’s speed, battery life and performance. Now the M6 can handle the MacBook’s AI capabilities, storage and high-resolution graphics. And for all of that power, most MacBooks are relatively thin and lightweight, making them easier for mobility — just a few of the reasons Apple users may be OK with paying more for what they’re getting.
Long battery life
Battery life is a big deal for many laptop buyers, and that’s another area where Apple delivers. Over a quarter of those surveyed (25.7%) said their MacBook’s battery life exceeds 10 hours — which is more than enough for a full day of work in most cases. And 18.7% say their MacBook’s battery lasts between 8 and 10 hours — totaling 44.4% of MacBook users saying their battery lasts 8 hours or more.
Comparatively, non-Apple laptop brands fall short in this category. Only 16.4% of Lenovo users say their laptop’s battery lasts at least 8 hours, and even fewer for Dell (12.7%) and HP (11.8%). If you’re leaning toward a MacBook for its battery life, CNET’s lab test shows that the MacBook Neo lasts 13 hours and 26 minutes for online streaming, whereas the Apple MacBook Air 13-inch M5 (2026 model) lasts 17 hours and 2 minutes.
Apple sweeps the brightness, color accuracy and clarity category with 99.2% of its users either satisfied or extremely satisfied with their laptop’s screen performance. No Apple users reported dissatisfaction.
“Apple has long been a favorite for creative professionals and content creators for good reason: Its MacBook displays are some of the best you’ll find on any laptop,” said Josh Goldman, CNET’s managing editor for computers. “While Apple may use marketing names like Retina and Liquid Retina to describe display features, they do translate into sharp and clear text and images, with excellent brightness, contrast, color gamut coverage and color accuracy.”
The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR even goes beyond what MacBook users have come to expect. It’s Apple’s first OLED touchscreen laptop and features next-level brightness, color and contrast.
High-grade design
Apple receives high ratings: 80% of MacBook owners say it has premium build quality, 18.2% say it’s solid, and those results don’t surprise us.
And MacBooks seem durable and reliable, with 87% of Apple users reporting no hardware failures on their MacBooks, while 8% say minor software fixes resolved their issues. Only 3% needed minor hardware repairs, and 2.2% needed major repairs — which could be fixes such as a battery or screen replacement.
Our editors say the M5 MacBook Air is thin and lightweight, but still has a well-built aluminum design. And the M5 Pro MacBook Pro is sturdy, too. What sets Apple’s laptop hardware apart could be its aluminum chassis — the casing that holds all of the components together.
“Apple makes three lines of MacBooks — the Neo, Air and Pro — and focuses on making those the best they can possibly be. They are all built to deliver a premium experience using high-quality materials, and that even includes the entry-level MacBook Neo,” said Goldman.
Lastly, Apple uses durable materials, such as the 100% recycled aluminum alloy it says encloses the 14-inch MacBook Pro. And the tech giant has several testing facilities to test MacBook durability.
Efficiency and productivity
When it comes to getting your daily tasks done, most CNET readers with MacBooks (70.9%) say Apple’s laptops handle workloads flawlessly. It’s worth noting that 45% use their MacBook for work tasks, but no Apple users reported poor performance.
Here’s why that might be: Apple’s laptops are packed with top-notch performance specs and features, like their powerful processors, unified memory and fast storage. Better processor performance means enhanced graphics, on-device AI capabilities and faster task speeds, all of which add up to being able to finish work, play games or stream videos without issues or lags caused by your laptop’s hardware.
On the software side, MacOS 27 Golden Gate gives you built-in AI features, like Siri AI and Visual Intelligence. And you can organize your Safari tabs by topic and use the Notify Me tool to be notified of website changes, like price drops or breaking news. Plus, you can create shortcuts to automate tasks. Coupling all of these features and specifications explains why Apple users rate MacBooks so highly for getting the job done.
The top chosen brand
Apple leads the way on brand retention with 68% of Apple users planning to buy the same MacBook model again, while 29.1% would buy another model from Apple’s lineup. Only 3% would switch to another brand that’s not Apple.
Usually, when you buy one Apple product, you’re likely to stick to the brand’s ecosystem, especially since Apple has its own operating systems to access its unique features and work seamlessly with other Apple products with Apple’s Continuity feature. For example, you can start an email on your iPhone, but finish typing it on your MacBook. Or you can call or send a text from your laptop without reaching for your iPhone. Other features work across Apple devices, including iCloud, Universal Clipboard and AirDrop.
Asus
Midrange-priced laptop
Asus wins as a midtier laptop choice with 67% of Asus owners paying between $500 and $1,499. There’s a sweet spot in this range with 38% spending between $500 and $999, and 28% paying between $1,000 and $1,499.
If you’re planning to spend that amount on a new laptop, you may also be pleased to know that Asus earns a higher satisfaction rating compared with other non-Apple laptop brands — 48% of Asus users say they’re extremely satisfied.
Asus laptops have a few features and specifications that may speak to that rating, regardless of budget. For example, the Zenbook A14 has a thin, lightweight design that’s rigid, with long battery life and an OLED display with strong contrast and color performance. This Copilot Plus PC sells for $1,600 (but retailers like Best Buy regularly have it on sale for less). Comparatively, these premium features from other brands could cost more or sacrifice important must-have features for the price.
Asus has other laptops worth exploring depending on your needs, like the budget-friendly Asus ZenBook S 14 or the premium Asus ROG Zephyrus G14 that could be good for gamers and creators.
Acer
Budget-friendly laptop
Over one-third of Acer laptop owners (38%) paid less than $500 for their laptop — which is greater than other laptop brands in this price range. Yet, 44% of Acer users say their laptop has exceptional value, while 50% say the value is fair — bringing a total positive cost-to-value score of over 94%. Acer also has an overall satisfaction score of 92.6% — the highest of non-Apple laptop brands.
If you’re impressed by Acer’s value and satisfaction scores, there are a few budget-friendly Acer options to consider. The Acer Aspire 16 AI wins CNET’s Editors’ Choice award. It has a big 16-inch screen but is still lightweight (3.5 pounds). And it has good battery life (over 21 hours on CNET’s battery drain test). There are a few other pluses, like the 1440p web camera that may be good for video conferencing and a sizable touchpad. All of those features and more add up to $700, which could make it a good computer for work or casual browsing. If you’re looking to spend slightly less, its predecessor, the Aspire 14 AI, is originally $639, but you may be able to score deals on both models during holiday sales.
These laptop brands are still worth considering
Even though Apple is highly recommended by CNET readers, there are plenty of other laptop models and brands worth considering depending on your needs. Here are a few non-Apple laptop brands that are runner-ups to CNET’s People’s Picks winners that you shouldn’t count out of your laptop search.
Lenovo
Battery life
Lenovo is best known for packing a powerful laptop into a compact design with tablet functionality, like its Yoga line, and its durable ThinkPad business models. But CNET readers with Lenovo laptops say the brand’s battery life stands out most compared with other non-MacBook laptops.
Survey findings show that 16% of Lenovo owners say their laptops can run for 8 hours or more. And 10.5% say their laptop battery lasts between 8 and 10 hours, while 6% say their Lenovo laptops can withstand at least 10 hours before needing a charge. That’s more than what readers say about other non-Apple brands. The Yoga 9i 2-in-1 Aura Edition lasts 25 hours and 45 minutes — making it one of the best laptop batteries CNET experts have tested.
Goldman said Lenovo has such a large and varied PC selection using the latest chips from Intel, AMD, Qualcomm and Nvidia that there is something for everyone and every budget. Even those who spend less on a Lenovo laptop can expect solid performance, including battery life.
High-grade design
If your laptop’s hardware fails or it breaks, you may be in the market for a new laptop sooner than expected. Think about cooling fan problems, overheating or your laptop not powering on at all. Over half (68%) of Lenovo laptop owners said they haven’t had any hardware issues with their laptops — the most compared to other non-MacBooks.
Beyond hardware durability, Lenovo also scores highly for its build and construction — overall making it a sturdy laptop choice. In our survey, 38% of Lenovo laptop owners say their laptop has a premium feel, while 51% say it’s solid — totaling a positive score of 89%.
If you’re looking for recommendations, the Lenovo Yoga Slim 7x Gen 11 has an all-metal design. And the Lenovo ThinkPad X1 Carbon Gen 14 is a business laptop with Lenovo’s well-known X1 Carbon exterior and new Space Frame design, which Elliott says makes it easier to repair or replace parts if needed.
The top chosen brand
Many Lenovo laptop users are loyal to the brand, which speaks to the overall positive satisfaction rating of 83%. If Lenovo owners were in the market for a new laptop, nearly three in four (73.2%) say they would buy another Lenovo laptop. Breaking down the percentage, 33.6% say they would buy the same model again. Meanwhile, 39.6% would buy a different model but stick to Lenovo.
Here’s why that might be. Lenovo offers a plethora of options to choose from based on your needs — while still evolving its laptops. For instance, the Lenovo Legion 5i Gen 10 has an open M.2 slot for a second storage drive and an OLED screen for crisp, colorful images — making it perfect for gaming. Its Yoga two-in-ones let you seamlessly switch between a tablet and traditional laptop, while Lenovo’s ThinkPad and ThinkBook business laptops offer everything from ultralight 2-pound bodies to expanding rollable screens. And its new designs don’t sacrifice the must-have needs like long battery life, durability and chip efficiency that lend to strong performance.
Asus
Value for the investment
Asus wins over nearly half of its laptop owners, with 47.5% giving it an exceptional value rating — exceeding expectations for its price. Take our Editors’ Choice pick, the Asus Zenbook A14. It’s super thin and lightweight, but it’s still sturdy thanks to its Ceralumnium body. Plus, it has supreme 24-hour battery life, 1TB of storage and an OLED display — all for $1,200. While that’s more expensive than some laptops, it’s what’s included in that price that makes it worthwhile compared with other non-Apple laptop brands.
Efficiency and productivity
Asus is the top non-Apple laptop option to consider for tasks, with 47.7% of CNET readers giving it high ratings. That’s followed by 40.4% of Asus laptop owners who say it has very good task performance. When it comes to tasks, 37% primarily use their Asus laptops for work, while 5% use theirs for gaming.
Asus is well known for having lightweight laptops with all-day-and-night battery life and stunning display quality. Asus laptops like the Asus ROG Zephyrus G16 have a good port selection, which could be good for gaming, work or simply connecting different devices without the need for additional adapters. And the Asus Zenbook S 14 has a strong neural processing unit that contributes to its high-speed AI performance.
Display quality
Asus scores highest for its screen brightness and clarity, with over half (51%) extremely satisfied with its screen quality and brightness, while 38.6% say they’re satisfied, giving Asus an overall satisfaction rate of 90%. One common thread we noticed in Asus laptops is their OLED screens, which deliver high-resolution video and graphics. Asus laptops also combine stunning display quality with excellent performance and at surprisingly low prices for all of their features.
For example, the Asus Zenbook 14 isn’t the highest-quality OLED we’ve seen, but it still produces clear text and graphics on a 14-inch screen, along with exceptional black levels, Elliott said. That’s still better than LCDs that many other non-MacBooks have, and could be the reason Asus owners rate it so highly in this category.
Dell
Premium laptop
Dell wins our readers over as a top choice for high-end laptops. One-third (33.3%) of Dell owners spent over $1,500, and of that percentage, 15.2% spent over $2,000.
Dell’s premium laptops largely cater to business and gaming with their standout features and performance. The Alienware 16X Aurora is Dell’s midrange gaming laptop with user-replaceable RAM, a bright display and strong performance for $2,280. But if you want more gaming features, Dell has the Alienware 16 Area-51, which has even better gaming performance, upgradable RAM and three SSD slots for $2,530. And if you’re looking for a non-Mac alternative that comes close to MacBook quality and performance, the higher-end Dell XPS 14 is the one to choose. It has the Intel Core Ultra X7 358H CPU, Intel Arc B390 graphics and 1TB of storage for $1,950.
Methodology
CNET commissioned Alchemer to conduct the People’s Picks survey to compile data. The survey was carried out online, and all figures are from Alchemer. The total sample comprised 1,003 adults. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 plus). Fieldwork was undertaken from Sept. 1 to Oct. 10, 2026.
results.summary:
Apple secured the top spot in CNET’s 2026 People’s Picks awards, outperforming competitors across eight categories including overall satisfaction, battery life, display quality, and hardware reliability.

### Key Points
- Apple achieved a 96.7% overall satisfaction rating, with 68% of MacBook owners stating they would purchase the same model again.
- Survey data indicates 44.4% of MacBook users experience battery life of eight hours or more, significantly outpacing Lenovo, Dell, and HP.
- Despite higher price points, 94.6% of Apple users reported that their laptops provide exceptional or fair value for the investment.
- Asus earned recognition as a top midrange choice, while Acer was highlighted for budget-friendly value and Lenovo for hardware durability.
- The survey, conducted by Alchemer, gathered insights from 1,003 U.S. adults between September and October 2026.

### Why it Matters
These findings highlight a strong consumer preference for premium hardware and ecosystem integration, which continues to drive high brand loyalty for Apple despite the availability of cheaper alternatives. For shoppers, the data suggests that while non-Apple brands like Asus and Acer offer competitive value and specific performance strengths, Apple remains the market leader in long-term user satisfaction and reliability.

results.title: China-Aligned Hackers Hijack Sogou Input Method DNS Requests to Deploy DarkVigil Backdoor
results.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
results.content:
A China-aligned threat actor known as SlippyNunchucks has been attributed to a Domain Name System (DNS) hijacking operation abusing insecure HTTP communications in Windows versions of Sogou Input Method as part of a surveillance campaign designed to deploy an implant called DarkVigil (aka FDMTP).
The campaign, observed starting July 1, 2026, is assessed to have targeted organizations and Chinese-speaking individuals in Hong Kong, Thailand, Japan, Vietnam, Oman, and Sri Lanka, according to ESET.
"DarkVigil implants are typically deployed through popular Chinese applications," ESET researcher Anh Ho said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "By abusing these applications, the SlippyNunchucks threat actor has been able to reach Chinese-speaking users across Asia and Europe."
Some of the applications abused by the adversary include Sogou Input Method, QuickFox, QingTalk, MiYunChat, SoftCam, and tawk.to.
Active since at least September 15, 2023, SlippyNunchucks is known for targeting organizations and Chinese-speaking individuals across South and East Asia. These attacks lead to the deployment of a modular .NET framework that includes DarkVigil and a set of over 20 plugins.
Although the use of the backdoor has been previously linked to Mustang Panda, ESET said it found no tactical overlaps between the threat actor and DarkVigil-related activity in its telemetry, prompting it to classify it as a distinct intrusion set.
Earlier this August, Fortinet's FortiGuard Incident Response Team detailed the threat actor's supply chain compromise of the QuickFox VPN and network acceleration tool to deliver DarkVigil.
According to the Slovakian cybersecurity company, the adversary shifted to exploiting Sogou Input Method, a popular Chinese-language input method editor developed by Tencent, as a delivery vector three days after QuickFox released a clean version of its program.
Specifically, the attack involves hijacking the app's branded vocabulary promotion mechanism to serve a malicious configuration, which ultimately paves the way for the deployment of the malware via SGTool.exe, a legitimate Sogou Input Method component that functions as a multi-purpose task dispatcher.
In a clean environment, the executable sends an HTTP request to the "config.pinyin.sogou[.]com/api/brandScd/getBrandScd.php" endpoint to fetch a configuration. But in the attack discovered by ESET, the DNS resolution of the domain is tampered with to resolve it to one of the two staging servers -
- 47.239.250[.]102 (sogou-cdn[.]com)
- 47.237.122[.]175 (dev.soft-png-cdn.com)
The consequence of this DNS hijacking was that HTTP requests to the "getBrandScd.php" endpoint were routed to one of the staging servers, which then responded with a malicious configuration. The configuration, for its part, instructs the binary to download two additional payloads from "sogou-cdn[.]com" and launch the malware via DLL sideloading -
- A legitimate Adobe executable ("biz_helper.exe")
- A rogue DLL ("libcef.dll") containing DarkVigil
DarkVigil is notable for its use of Duplex Message Transport Protocol (DMTP) for command-and-control (C2), allowing the client to execute and orchestrate plugins received from an attacker-controlled server to facilitate persistence or data collection.
Following responsible disclosure, Tencent addressed the vulnerability (CVE-2026-120422) in version 16.10, released on October 29, 2026, by migrating the affected HTTP requests to HTTPS.
SlippyNunchucks is suspected to operate keeping the interests of the Chinese government in mind, with ESET describing it as a nation-state surveillance effort.
"Although SlippyNunchucks targets organizations and individuals across multiple sectors, we discovered significant surveillance activity against an organization operating Chinese-language online betting platforms in Sri Lanka, Hong Kong, and the Philippines," ESET said.
"The targeting of this organization is notable given China's restrictions on gambling, including criminal penalties for operating gambling businesses and organizing Chinese citizens to gamble abroad."
This is not the first time China-nexus threat actors have weaponized the Sogou Input Method as an entry point for malware distribution. In September 2026, Gen Digital said a now-patched vulnerability in the input method editor (CVE-2026-51990) was exploited by UNC3569 to deliver a backdoor dubbed GRAYRABBIT by means of a crafted link.
"The vulnerability chains three separate weaknesses into a single, one-click exploit: unvalidated command-line argument injection in the sgbiz: custom protocol handler, unrestricted URL navigation in a CEF-based WebView, and a severely outdated, unsandboxed Chromium browser engine [susceptible to CVE-2021-38003]," Gen Digital said.
results.summary:
The China-aligned threat actor SlippyNunchucks is exploiting insecure HTTP communications in the Sogou Input Method to deploy the DarkVigil surveillance implant across multiple Asian and European nations.

### Key Points
- SlippyNunchucks has targeted organizations and individuals in Hong Kong, Thailand, Japan, Vietnam, Oman, and Sri Lanka since July 2026.
- The attack uses DNS hijacking to intercept HTTP requests and deliver malicious configurations via the legitimate Sogou component SGTool.exe.
- DarkVigil is a modular .NET framework that utilizes over 20 plugins and the Duplex Message Transport Protocol for command-and-control operations.
- Other applications compromised by the group include QuickFox, QingTalk, MiYunChat, SoftCam, and tawk.to.
- Tencent patched the underlying vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-120422, in version 16.10 of the Sogou Input Method on October 29, 2026.

### Why it Matters
This campaign highlights the significant risks posed by supply chain compromises that weaponize widely used, trusted software to bypass traditional security perimeters. By forcing a transition from insecure HTTP to encrypted HTTPS, the patch mitigates this specific vector, but the incident underscores the ongoing threat of nation-state actors targeting Chinese-speaking populations globally.

results.title: SpaceX joins forces with Qualcomm to build Starlink Mobile 5G network
results.author: James Rogerson
results.content:
- Qualcomm's Dragonwing Cellular Infrastructure platforms will support Starlink Mobile's terrestrial base stations
- This tech will help improve coverage, capacity, and spectral efficiency
- However, analysts argue that spectrum and tower leases are more important for the carrier
Starlink Mobile has just taken another big step towards launching its US mobile network to compete with the likes of Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile — the SpaceX-owned company has announced that Qualcomm’s Dragonwing Cellular Infrastructure platforms will support the carrier’s terrestrial base stations.
According to Qualcomm, these base stations are “designed to improve coverage, capacity and spectral efficiency, helping the network serve more traffic efficiently.”
The multi-year agreement will see Qualcomm's tech used in "tens of thousands of sites", with the rollout due to begin in 2027. Qualcomm has described the agreement as its "biggest 5G deal yet".
In a post on X Elon Musk claimed that “Qualcomm’s technology is excellent,” adding in another that “at last there will be one network with good signal everywhere!”
However, despite rumors from The Washington Post that SpaceX is also looking to acquire Boost Mobile from EchoStar, telecoms experts say the move is just one step on a potentially long battle with the established mobile giants.
Analysis: A small step in a long bid to 'disrupt the entire industry'
So how big a deal is this? Telecoms analyst Tim Farrar, President at TMF Associates, told us: "This deal is an important part of building a new mobile network in the US. But even more important will be for Starlink to secure the spectrum and tower leases that will be used with the Qualcomm equipment.
"I think a purchase of the remaining EchoStar spectrum assets and a settlement with the tower companies is the easiest and quickest way to go about that, especially as Starlink intends to start deploying equipment next year."
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
By “EchoStar spectrum assets,” Farrar is referring to the parent company of Boost Mobile, which was the subject of those acquisition rumors from The Washington Post. However, Boost Mobile has MVNO (mobile virtual network operator) agreements with T-Mobile and AT&T, and according to a research note from MoffettNathanson (via TeleCompetitor) it’s unlikely that those agreements would be transferred to Starlink Mobile.
In other words, that “settlement with the tower companies” mentioned by Farrar could still be a stumbling block, especially since Starlink Mobile was recently turned down as an MVNO by the US’s major carriers. It remains unclear how easy it will be able to lease towers.
Without that, Starlink Mobile will have spectrum but not much in the way of ground-based infrastructure, leaving it with the big and expensive job of rolling out its own.
The fourth big mobile giant?
Other analysts are more bullish about Starlink Mobile's prospects. “The new agreement between SpaceX and Qualcomm reinforces the likelihood that Starlink Mobile could become a credible fourth nationwide mobile network provider in the U.S," said Mike Dano, Lead Industry Analyst at Ookla.
However, he also added a note of caution. "Of course, there are many more steps along this path, including building radios for a Starlink Mobile terrestrial network, putting them on top of towers, and then activating services for paying customers. And even then, it’s not clear whether Starlink Mobile will be able to successfully compete against the market’s established mobile providers," Dano added.
"I think it will take several years — at the very, very least — for Starlink Mobile to build the terrestrial network and launch the new satellites that will be necessary for it to potentially become a credible fourth nationwide mobile network provider," he added.
Elon Musk's claims that Starlink Mobile will be the "one network with good signal everywhere" also don't currently match reality. Dano pointed towards Ookla's recent research on Starlink Mobile's 'direct to device' (D2D) offering. While Starlink was praised for filling coverage gaps in the US, the report concluded that "Starlink Mobile’s network trails the performance of terrestrial networks".
For example, Ookla's tests concluded one in seven Starlink Mobile D2D texts failed to go through, compared with around one in fifty on the terrestrial network. "This is the kind of performance gap that Starlink Mobile will need to address with its terrestrial network buildout,” Dano added.
Other mobile networks, meanwhile, think Elon Musk is playing a long game. "It's about getting enough network coverage to fundamentally disrupt the economics of the entire industry," said Peter Adderton, CEO of MobileX and founder of Boost Mobile in a post on X.
"I think the endgame isn't simply competing with the MNOs, but weakening their economics and valuations to a point where SpaceX can eventually acquire one at a fraction of today's valuation? This isn't necessarily just about winning wireless customers. It's about changing the economics of wireless itself," he added.

And of course you can also follow TechRadar on TikTok for news, reviews, unboxings in video form, and get regular updates from us on WhatsApp too.
James is a freelance phones, tablets and wearables writer and sub-editor at TechRadar. He has a love for everything ‘smart’, from watches to lights, and can often be found arguing with AI assistants or drowning in the latest apps. James also contributes to 3G.co.uk, 4G.co.uk and 5G.co.uk and has written for T3, Digital Camera World, Clarity Media and others, with work on the web, in print and on TV.

### Key Points

results.title: Qualcomm and SpaceX ink a deal to begin working on a Starlink 5G network for 2027
results.author: nickodiaz@sbcglobal.net (Nickolas Diaz) , Nickolas Diaz
results.content:
What you need to know
- Qualcomm announced that it's inked a deal with SpaceX to begin creating a 5G Starlink mobile network, with plans to debut in 2027.
- Qualcomm states it views this deal as a chance to build "world-leading cellular infrastructure" in the U.S. to advance 5G with SpaceX.
- It's worth remembering that, a week ago, T-Mobile reportedly denied becoming wireless partners with SpaceX's Starlink network.
Qualcomm announced major next steps in a partnership with SpaceX for a mobile network that's eyeing a 2027 debut in the U.S — not to mention plans for a next-gen,, AI-native 6G network.
Qualcomm will help SpaceX build a "high-capacity 5G" network that's "built for scale," the company announced Wed., Nov. 4. To achieve this, Starlink Mobile will reportedly utilize Massive MIMO radio units. Qualcomm explains this technology will bring "advanced antenna capabilities to its terrestrial network." Without getting too technical, Qualcomm states this tech is necessary to improve Starlink's mobile coverage and efficiency to handle its network traffic.

The cellular network effectively drew the line at helping SpaceX develop its own 5G network, turning it into a "wireless partner."
It was reported that "Such a deal would let SpaceX offer wireless services on top of T-Mobile's existing cell network, paving an easier route into the U.S. mobile market for the satellite company." However, CEO Srini Gopalan said T-Mobile evaluates partnerships based on distribution channels, the ability to open new addressable markets, and more.

results.title: Canva To Cut Or Relocate 22% of Global Workforce
results.author: BeauHD
results.content:

The changes mirror a trend across the technology sector, where software companies are fighting to stay competitive against cheaper artificial intelligence disrupters while aggressively embedding AI tools themselves.
[...] The restructure will affect 1,271 people, according to the company, as it focuses on "collapsing layers" and bringing "more teams together in person." [...] Those leaving Canva will receive at least six months of salary and retain healthcare coverage for a further 12 months in countries where workers receive that benefit. results.title: BitMart founder says security team ‘severely understaffed’ after new hack
results.author: Cointelegraph by Nate Kostar
results.content:
BitMart founder says security team ‘severely understaffed’ after new hack
The crypto exchange’s founder warned of security staffing shortages amid restructuring as analysts flagged suspicious transfers potentially linked to the Mercado Bitcoin hack.
Cryptocurrency exchange BitMart is operating with an understaffed security team following restructuring, its founder said Wednesday, after confirming a new hack that may be linked to the recent attack on Brazil’s exchange Mercado Bitcoin.
In a post on X, BitMart founder Sheldon Xia said threats against employees and alleged retaliation by former staff had complicated efforts to retain technical personnel.
“It took considerable effort and individual conversations to persuade some key technical staff to remain and maintain our core systems,” Xia wrote. “However, we continue to face numerous attacks. Our security team is currently severely understaffed, but we are still doing everything we can to safeguard data and assets.”
Xia described the amount involved in Monday’s hack as small but did not disclose a figure. Blockchain analytics firm Bitquery identified approximately $391,000 in suspicious transfers from wallets mostly associated with BitMart across three blockchains, according to a Wednesday investigation.
Source: Sheldon Xia
Bitquery traced the funds to a wallet also implicated in the more than $46 million Mercado Bitcoin hack on Monday, Nov. 2, supporting Xia’s preliminary suspicion of a possible connection between the incidents.
Related: North Korea denies role in $6.3B Binance hack, points finger at US
BitMart weighs restructuring after shutdown announcement
The latest breach comes amid months of uncertainty over BitMart’s future. The exchange announced in July that it would end trading on Aug. 26 and cease operations in January 2027. Following the announcement, users reported delayed withdrawals and frozen accounts, raising concerns about access to their funds.
In August, BitMart’s Chinese-language X account alleged that employees had gone unpaid and demanded answers about customer funds. The founder dismissed the allegations as fabricated, though it remained unclear who controlled the account at the time.
In a restructuring proposal published Monday, the exchange outlined three potential recovery options for users, including liquid asset distributions and recovery-linked tokens, with plans to seek court approval in December or January.
Cointelegraph contacted BitMart for details about the restructuring, security staffing and latest breach but had not received a response by publication.
Crypto crime-fighting alliance disbands amid wave of hacks
Separately, a crypto crime-fighting alliance formed by Tron, Tether and TRM Labs has dissolved amid a wave of major industry hacks, Bloomberg reported Wednesday.
The T3 Financial Crime Unit, launched in September 2024 and later joined by Binance, struggled with slow responses and poor coordination, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter. One source said the group disbanded in late August.
In May, T3 said it had helped freeze more than $450 million in assets linked to suspected criminal activity since its launch in 2024.
The group’s dissolution comes amid a wave of major crypto hacks, including last week’s $6.3 billion Binance breach, the largest cryptocurrency theft on record.
Magazine: Wall Street killed Bitcoin’s wild rallies: 10x’s Markus Thielen
results.summary:
BitMart founder Sheldon Xia confirmed the cryptocurrency exchange is operating with a severely understaffed security team following a new hack linked to the recent Mercado Bitcoin breach.

### Key Points
- Blockchain analytics firm Bitquery identified approximately $391,000 in suspicious transfers from BitMart wallets across three blockchains.
- The stolen funds were traced to a wallet previously implicated in the $46 million hack of Brazil-based exchange Mercado Bitcoin.
- BitMart is currently undergoing a restructuring process, with plans to cease all operations by January 2027.
- Founder Sheldon Xia cited employee threats and internal retaliation as primary factors complicating the retention of essential technical security staff.
- The exchange has proposed recovery options for users, including liquid asset distributions, pending court approval expected between December and January.

### Why it Matters
This security breach highlights the operational instability of an exchange already facing a planned shutdown and ongoing user withdrawal delays. The incident underscores the broader risks to customer assets when financial platforms struggle with internal staffing shortages and organizational restructuring during periods of high cyber threat activity.

results.title: Fate of the Galaxy is a huge, fully-featured Star Wars space combat sim that, thanks to being a total conversion mod for Freespace Open, even runs on my rubbish laptop
results.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
results.content:
Star Wars has been back in the news recently because, to cut a long story short, the US alt-right have decided that Darth Vader was actually the good guy. We are not here to indulge such buffoonery. We are here to talk about Fate of the Galaxy, a free unofficial space combat simulator set during the events of the original Star Wars trilogy, featuring several mission-based campaigns and a stable of Imperial and Rebel Alliance ships that ranges from the quad-blasting X-Wing to Boba Fett's Firespray 31. Also, Naboo starfighters, if you really must.
It's a total conversion of poor dead Volition's venerable dogfighter FreeSpace 2, running on the open source Free Space 2 Open engine via the popular Knossos launcher. You don't need a copy of FreeSpace 2 to play it. You also don't need to pay. And nor do you need a whizbang PC – this bucket of bolts hums along happily on my i5-1145G7 with no dedicated graphics card. As the Rancor said to the padawan: finally, some good food.
Fate of the Galaxy has been in development off and on for almost two decades, weathering a number of team changes and shifts of focus. The FreeSpace Wiki has a longer account of its travels. It's not an officially licensed Star Wars production, as made evident by a scrolling text intro which takes the official orchestral theme and moves every note up or down a place, as though spitefully jolting the piano around under John Williams' fingers. It's not quite as bizarre as Portsmouth Sinfonia's Also sprach Zarathustra but it did make me cackle like the Emperor contemplating a freshly made asteroid field. But then I began playing, and my presumptuous merriment became a frown of concentration.
While hardly Steel Battalion, Fate of the Galaxy is a proper nerdy sim with a bustling 3D cockpit and all sorts of keyboard shortcuts to try once and immediately forget. You'll need to funnel energy between fore and aft shields during bombing runs on Star Destroyers, target individual subsystems with your ion cannon, give orders to other pilots, and consider whether to synch different guns for maximum effect. I can run the game fine on my work laptop with integrated graphics, but I'm definitely feeling the need for a beefier keyboard. And also a joystick. Certainly, I'm not going to get far in LAN multiplayer with this hunk of junk.
It seems a very generous production, based on 30 minutes playing kiss-chase with TIE bombers. The story campaigns and quickfix stand-alone skirmishes aside, there's a mission editor with text-based files for easier sharing. There's also VR support with head-tracking, should you own one of those haunted helmets. Learn more via the online manual (Google Doc), and find Fate of the Galaxy itself on Moddb. You'll need around seven gigs of disc space.
This being the year 2026, there's the question of generative AI usage - a topic of much concern lately in modding circles. Fate of the Galaxy's official site boasts that all the visual assets were "made by humans only". I'm less sure about other aspects – there's seemingly some artificial VO during the tutorial, though it sounds like antiquated, less insidious robocaller software. The FreeSpace Open engine itself greatly pre-dates today's chatbot invasion. The original FreeSpace 2 launched in 1999 - a more civilised age, when everybody still thought Darth Vader was an arsehole.
results.summary:
Fate of the Galaxy is a free, fan-made space combat simulator built on the FreeSpace 2 Open engine that allows players to pilot iconic Star Wars starships in missions.

### Key Points
- The game is a total conversion mod of the 1999 title FreeSpace 2 and does not require the original game to play.
- It features multiple mission-based campaigns, standalone skirmishes, a mission editor, and support for VR with head-tracking.
- The simulator is optimized for low-end hardware and runs on systems without dedicated graphics cards.
- Developers confirmed that all visual assets were created by humans, avoiding the use of generative AI for graphics.
- Players can download the seven-gigabyte project via Moddb and access documentation through an online manual.

### Why it Matters
This project demonstrates the longevity of the open-source FreeSpace 2 engine and the enduring popularity of community-driven Star Wars game development. It provides a accessible, high-fidelity alternative for fans seeking a complex space combat simulation without the need for modern high-end hardware.

results.title: Apple Will Check Public iCloud Links for Harmful Content Starting in iOS 27.3
results.author: Juli Clover
results.content:
Apple says it will start checking public iCloud links for harmful content in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3.
Images in iCloud Photos and files in iCloud Drive shared using the "Anyone with the link" option will be "made accessible to Apple" for a content check. Apple doesn't define harmful content, but it could mean malware, malicious files, and/or child sexual abuse material (CSAM) given Apple's mention of law enforcement involvement.
If you try to upload harmful content, Apple reserves the right to move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete the content at any time. Apple may also take action against your Apple Account, including blocking or disabling your Apple Account, blocking the ability to create a new Apple Account with the associated email address or phone number, or if necessary, involving law enforcement.
iCloud files can be shared with "Send a Copy," which sends a file directly, or "Share a Link," which lets someone download it. Link sharing options are "People you choose" or "Anyone with the link," and it's only the latter option that will be evaluated by Apple.
Apple does not say whether links created before the 27.3 updates will be checked.
Apple says content made available to anyone is no longer end-to-end encrypted, even when Advanced Data Protection is on.
iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3 are currently available to developers for beta testing, and the software will see a public release in December.
results.summary:
Apple will begin scanning public iCloud links for harmful content in upcoming software updates for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS, scheduled for a public release this December.

### Key Points
- Apple will monitor files and photos shared via the "Anyone with the link" option in iCloud Drive and iCloud Photos.
- The policy applies to iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3, which are currently in developer beta.
- Content identified as harmful may be removed, and Apple reserves the right to disable associated user accounts or contact law enforcement.
- Files shared publicly are no longer end-to-end encrypted, even for users who have enabled Advanced Data Protection.
- The new scanning protocols specifically target public links rather than files shared with restricted groups or "Send a Copy" transfers.

### Why it Matters
This update marks a significant shift in Apple's privacy policy by removing end-to-end encryption for publicly shared iCloud content to facilitate automated safety checks. Users must now be aware that files accessible via public links are subject to Apple's content moderation and potential account-level enforcement actions.
